nameStory: The 'Unequal' Cellophane Bee gets its name from the uneven or asymmetrical markings on its body, which help distinguish it from its many cellophane bee cousins. These bees are called 'cellophane' bees because they line their underground nest cells with a clear, waterproof secretion that looks and feels remarkably like thin plastic wrap or cellophane.
description: The Unequal Cellophane Bee is a medium-sized native bee that's an important early-season pollinator in New England. These fuzzy, brownish-black bees are about the size of a small honeybee and are most active in spring when maple and willow trees are blooming. Unlike honeybees, they're solitary creatures that dig individual burrows in the ground rather than living in hives. You'll often see them busy at work on fruit trees and early spring flowers, methodically collecting pollen and nectar.

idTips.label: Ground nesting behavior
idTips.description: Look for small mounds of fresh soil with penny-sized holes, often in sandy or well-drained areas where females dig their burrows

idTips.label: Fuzzy brown-black body
idTips.description: Medium-sized bee with dense, soft hair covering a dark brown to black body, giving it a slightly fuzzy teddy bear appearance

idTips.label: Spring tree preference
idTips.description: Often seen visiting red maple, willow, and apple blossoms in early spring, moving methodically from flower to flower

idTips.label: Solitary flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies alone rather than in groups, with a steady, purposeful flight style as it moves between flowers and nesting sites

idTips.label: Cellophane nest lining
idTips.description: If you find their nests, the cells are lined with a clear, waterproof material that feels smooth and plastic-like to the touch

habitat: Look for Unequal Cellophane Bees in areas with well-drained, sandy or loamy soil where they can easily dig their burrows, such as south-facing slopes, garden edges, and open woodlands. They're often found near early-blooming trees like red maples, willows, and apple orchards. You'll spot them from lowland areas up to moderate elevations throughout New England, especially in locations that get good morning sun.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity time! Adults emerge and are most visible from April through May, busily visiting maple, willow, and apple blossoms. Look for fresh soil mounds with small holes indicating active nesting.
seasonality.summer: Adults have largely finished their lifecycle by early summer, but you might still see evidence of their nesting burrows in sandy soil areas.
seasonality.fall: Largely inactive, with new generation developing underground in their cellophane-lined cells.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae in their underground burrows, completely out of sight until spring emergence.

funFact: These industrious bees are nature's original plastic manufacturers – they actually produce their own waterproof polymer to line their nest cells, creating a material so similar to synthetic cellophane that early scientists were amazed by the resemblance!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark, fuzzy spring bees like mining bees, but cellophane bees have a distinctive methodical, business-like way of moving on flowers and their nest holes are typically cleaner and more perfectly round. Memory trick: 'Cellophane bees are clean' – their nest entrances look neat and tidy compared to the messier soil piles of mining bees.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these native cellophane bees with non-native honeybees or bumblebees. While they're sometimes called 'polyester bees' by scientists because of their plastic-like nest lining, this can be confusing since they don't actually use synthetic materials – they make their own natural version of plastic!
compareHints: Among New England's cellophane bees, the Unequal Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its preference for early spring tree blossoms, especially maples and willows, while relatives like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee specialize in late-season flowers. It's also one of the more common and widespread species in the genus, making it the cellophane bee you're most likely to encounter in spring orchards and maple groves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cellophane bees, the rufous-backed stands out for its prominent rusty-red thoracic hair, while most relatives like the unequal cellophane bee have more subdued brown or gray coloring.
Among New England's cellophane bees, the Spine-shouldered stands out primarily due to its namesake shoulder spines, which most relatives lack.

Unlike the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee which specializes on late-summer flowers, or the Aster Cellophane Bee found on fall composites, the Blueberry Cellophane Bee is strictly a spring specialist of heath family plants.

Among New England's cellophane bees, the Aster Cellophane Bee is distinguished by its late-season activity and aster specialization, while the Unequal Cellophane Bee flies much earlier in spring when fruit trees bloom.

Among New England's dozen cellophane bee species, the Broad-footed stands out with its notably wide tarsi, while species like the Goldenrod Cellophane Bee or Aster Cellophane Bee are named for their flower preferences rather than physical features.
